lead: Commutation is turning off a conducting SCR. Because the gate cannot do it, the circuit must bring the anode current below the holding current and then keep the SCR reverse-biased long enough for it to recover its blocking ability. In AC circuits the supply does this by itself every half-cycle (natural commutation). In DC circuits the current never falls by itself, so a capacitor, a resonant circuit or another switch must force it to zero (forced commutation). The one design rule behind all methods is that the circuit turn-off time must exceed the device turn-off time.
prereq: You need: holding current and the two-transistor model from the SCR chapter.

blocks.text: An SCR is latched while its anode current stays above the holding current I<sub>H</sub>: the two internal transistors keep each other on. To turn it off, the anode current must fall below I<sub>H</sub>, and the stored charge in the layers must then disappear before forward voltage returns.

items: Natural (line) commutation: with an AC supply the anode voltage reverses every half-cycle, the current falls to zero and the SCR is reverse-biased for the rest of that half-cycle. No extra parts are needed. It is used in controlled rectifiers, AC voltage controllers and cycloconverters. It is also called class F commutation.

Forced commutation: with a DC supply the current does not fall, so an external circuit, usually a charged capacitor, is switched to reverse-bias the SCR and divert its current. It is used in DC choppers and in SCR inverters. Classes A to E are forced methods.

sections.h3: Circuit turn-off time and device turn-off time

blocks.text: The device turn-off time t<sub>q</sub> (from the datasheet) is the time from current zero until the SCR can block forward voltage again; it is about 10 µs to 20 µs for fast (inverter-grade) SCRs and 50 µs to a few hundred microseconds for converter-grade ones, and it grows with junction temperature. The circuit turn-off time t<sub>c</sub> is the time for which the circuit actually holds the SCR reverse-biased after its current reaches zero. Commutation succeeds only if t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub>, usually with a margin of 1.2 to 1.5. If t<sub>c</sub> is too short, the SCR turns on again as soon as forward voltage returns.

blocks.where: for a capacitor of C farads, charged to V volts, placed across the SCR to commutate a load current of I amperes that stays constant during commutation (true for an inductive load). The capacitor voltage, which is the reverse voltage on the SCR, falls linearly from −V to zero in t<sub>c</sub> seconds. Turned round, it gives the design rule C ≥ I t<sub>c</sub> / V.

blocks.text: In class C with resistive loads R1 and R2, the capacitor voltage seen by the SCR being turned off swings from −V towards +V through R1, so t<sub>c</sub> = R1 C ln 2 = 0.693 R1 C, not C V / I. In class D the load current discharges the capacitor at a constant rate, so t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I applies.

examples.question: An impulse-commutated (class D) chopper has a commutating capacitor C = 1 µF charged to 200 V. The load current, constant during commutation, is 5 A. The SCR has t<sub>q</sub> = 30 µs. Find t<sub>c</sub> and say whether commutation succeeds.
steps: Rate at which the load current discharges the capacitor: dv/dt = I / C = 5 A ÷ 1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F = 5 V/µs.
The SCR voltage rises from −200 V to 0 at 5 V/µs: t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I = 1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 200 ÷ 5 = 4 × 10<sup>−5</sup> s = 40 µs.
Compare: t<sub>c</sub> = 40 µs > t<sub>q</sub> = 30 µs, a margin of 40 ÷ 30 = 1.33.
examples.answer: t<sub>c</sub> = 40 µs, which exceeds t<sub>q</sub> = 30 µs, so the SCR turns off.

examples.question: Design the commutating capacitor for a class D chopper on V = 220 V with a load current of 50 A. The SCR has t<sub>q</sub> = 30 µs; use a safety factor of 1.5.
steps: Required circuit turn-off time: t<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 × 30 µs = 45 µs.
Choose the next standard value, 12 µF, rated above 220 V.
Check: t<sub>c</sub> = 12 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 220 ÷ 50 = 52.8 µs, which is 1.76 × t<sub>q</sub>.
examples.answer: C = 12 µF gives t<sub>c</sub> = 52.8 µs, comfortably above 45 µs.

traps: Current zero is not turn-off. The SCR must also stay reverse-biased for longer than t<sub>q</sub>.
t<sub>c</sub> belongs to the circuit, t<sub>q</sub> to the device. A bigger capacitor lengthens t<sub>c</sub>; nothing in the circuit shortens t<sub>q</sub>, except keeping the junction cool.
Using t<sub>c</sub> = C V / I for class C with resistive loads: there t<sub>c</sub> = 0.693 R1 C. For R1 = 50 Ω and C = 1 µF that is 34.7 µs.
Class A is self or load commutation and class B is resonant pulse; do not swap them.
Natural commutation cannot turn off an SCR fed from DC: the DC current never reaches zero by itself.

quiz.a: The process of turning off a conducting SCR: reducing its anode current below the holding current and keeping it reverse-biased until it regains forward blocking.

quiz.q: State the condition for successful commutation.
quiz.a: The circuit turn-off time must exceed the device turn-off time, t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub>, usually by a factor of 1.2 to 1.5.

quiz.q: Why can natural commutation work only with an AC supply?
quiz.a: Only an AC supply reverses the anode voltage by itself, which takes the current to zero and holds reverse bias for the rest of the half-cycle. A DC supply never does, so the current must be forced to zero.
A self or load; B resonant pulse; C complementary; D impulse or auxiliary; E external pulse; F line (natural).

quiz.q: A capacitor of 2 µF charged to 150 V commutates a constant 3 A load current. The SCR has t<sub>q</sub> = 60 µs. Does it turn off?
quiz.a: t<sub>c</sub> = 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 150 ÷ 3 = 100 µs > 60 µs, so it turns off, with a margin of 1.67.

quiz.q: In complementary commutation the load resistor of the SCR being turned off is 50 Ω and C = 1 µF. Find t<sub>c</sub>.
A student says ‘the SCR turns off as soon as its current reaches zero’. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Current zero only starts turn-off. Stored charge must recombine while the SCR is reverse-biased; if forward voltage returns before t<sub>q</sub> has passed, the SCR turns on again without a gate pulse.

quiz.q: A chopper that works at 25 °C fails to commutate after an hour at full load. Explain.
quiz.a: t<sub>q</sub> rises with junction temperature. When the SCR heats up, t<sub>q</sub> grows above the circuit turn-off time t<sub>c</sub>, so the SCR re-triggers when forward voltage returns. Fixes: a larger C, a lower load current, a faster SCR or better cooling.

beyond: Not for the exam. Forced-commutated SCR choppers and inverters have been replaced by IGBTs and MOSFETs, which the gate can turn off. The idea of t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub> survives in line-commutated HVDC converters, where the inverter must keep enough extinction angle, and in soft-switching converters that create a zero-current window for the switch. Search for ‘extinction angle HVDC inverter’ and ‘zero-current switching’.
